basisOfRecord.quote: To determine whether plantation forestry drives functional homogenization of soil biota, we compared the taxonomic and functional diversity of ants and springtails between natural (indigenous forests and grasslands) and transformed (Eucalyptus plantations) biotopes.
Using pitfall trapping, four 300 ml plastic cups (9.5 cm diameter and 8 cm deep) were placed in $\mathrm { ~ a ~ 2 ~ m ~ } ^ { 2 }$ grid at each site.
Secondly, arthropods were collected directly using an aspirator within a randomly placed 1 m quadrat of each site.

For ants, traits used in the analysis (Table S2) were derived from the literature (eye size, habitat position and feeding strategy) (Table S3) or measured in the laboratory (body length, femur length and darkness of the integument).
Figure S1 Species accumulation curves of all species collected across all biotopes (indigenous forest, grassland, pine and eucalypt compartments) in the Midlands and Zululand.
Midlands samples consisted of 15 678 ant individuals, in 87 morphospecies in 19 genera in six sub-families.
Zululand samples consisted of 10 053 ant individuals, consisting of 74 morphospecies in 25 genera in 6 sub-families.
For springtails, Midlands samples consisted of 63 719 individuals, in 87 morphospecies in 11 families and three orders.
Zululand’s samples consisted of 5119 springtail individuals, in 47 morphospecies in 11 families and 3 orders.

measurementStatistic.quote: The prevalence of morphological and ecological traits in natural vs. transformed biotopes was also assessed.
Where possible, six individuals per species were measured, and an average body length (for both taxa), and femur length (for ants only) was estimated.
For polymorphic ants, individuals of varying sizes were selected, and an average body length calculated for those species.
Traits used for the calculation of functional richness and Rao’s quadratic entropy for ants (Table S2) and springtails (Table S4) are provided.
